## The reference triangle

All element computations happen on the reference triangle $\hat T$ with
vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$. A physical triangle $T$ with vertices
$x_1, x_2, x_3$ is its image under the affine map

$$
F_T(\hat x) = x_1 + B_T \hat x, \qquad B_T = [\, x_2 - x_1 \;\; x_3 - x_1 \,].
$$

Counterclockwise orientation means $\det B_T > 0$, and $|T| = \det B_T / 2$.
Gradients transform with the inverse transpose,
$\nabla \phi = B_T^{-T} \hat\nabla \hat\phi$, and integrals pick up the factor
$\det B_T$.

## Lagrange basis functions

With barycentric coordinates $\lambda_1 = 1 - \xi - \eta$,
$\lambda_2 = \xi$, $\lambda_3 = \eta$:

* **P1**: $\phi_i = \lambda_i$, nodes at the vertices;
* **P2**: $\phi_i = \lambda_i(2\lambda_i - 1)$ at the vertices and
  $4\lambda_1\lambda_2$, $4\lambda_2\lambda_3$, $4\lambda_3\lambda_1$ at the
  midpoints of the local edges.

Both satisfy the nodal property $\phi_i(x_j) = \delta_{ij}$:

```{r}
p1 <- fe_element(1)
p1$basis(p1$nodes[, 1], p1$nodes[, 2])
p2 <- fe_element(2)
round(p2$basis(p2$nodes[, 1], p2$nodes[, 2]), 12)
```

Gradients are available analytically and are checked against finite
differences in the test suite:

```{r}
g <- p2$grad(0.2, 0.3)
rbind(xi = g$xi, eta = g$eta)
```

The closed-form P1 element matrices serve as independent references:

$$
K_T = |T|\, G G^\top, \qquad M_T = \frac{|T|}{12}\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\1&2&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix},
$$

where the rows of $G$ are the constant gradients of the three basis functions.

```{r}
v <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(2, 0), c(0, 1))
element_stiffness_p1(v)
element_mass_p1(v)
```

## Function spaces and degrees of freedom

`fe_space()` builds the global continuous space. P1 degrees of freedom are
the mesh nodes; P2 adds one per edge, numbered after the nodes.

```{r}
mesh <- pde_mesh_rectangle(nx = 3)
V1 <- fe_space(mesh, 1); V2 <- fe_space(mesh, 2)
c(P1 = V1$ndof, P2 = V2$ndof, nodes = nrow(mesh$nodes), edges = nrow(mesh$edges))
head(V2$cell_dofs, 3)
boundary_dofs(V2, "bottom")
```

## Finite-element functions

`interpolate()` computes the nodal interpolant; `evaluate()` returns values
and gradients at arbitrary points (points are located with a bucket grid).

```{r}
u <- interpolate(function(x, y) exp(x) * cos(2 * y), V2)
evaluate(u, c(0.3, 0.7), c(0.2, 0.9), gradient = TRUE)
c(exact = exp(0.3) * cos(0.4))
plot(u)
```

`evaluation_matrix()` returns the sparse matrix $P$ with $P\mathbf U$ equal
to point values; it is the observation operator of inverse problems.

## Quadrature

Element integrals use Gaussian rules on the reference triangle.
`quadrature_triangle(d)` is exact for polynomials of total degree $d$:
1 point for $d \le 1$, 3 points for $d = 2$, the 7-point Radon rule for
$d \le 5$, and collapsed Gauss-Legendre products beyond. `quadrature_interval(n)`
is the $n$-point Gauss-Legendre rule, exact to degree $2n - 1$.

The exact monomial integral over $\hat T$ is
$\int_{\hat T} \xi^i \eta^j = i!\,j!/(i+j+2)!$:

```{r}
q <- quadrature_triangle(5)
q
c(rule = sum(q$weights * q$points[, 1]^2 * q$points[, 2]^3),
  exact = factorial(2) * factorial(3) / factorial(7))
```

The assembly default is degree $2p + 2$ for elements of degree $p$: exact for
mass matrices with affine coefficients and for stiffness matrices with
quadratic coefficients. Error norms use degree $2p + 4$. A rule that is too
coarse for the data would add a quadrature error to the discretization error,
so the defaults are deliberately generous.

`integrate_mesh()` integrates any function over a mesh:

```{r}
integrate_mesh(pde_mesh_rectangle(nx = 4), function(x, y) x^3 * y^2, degree = 5)
1 / 12
```
